title: Leadership by Example: The Davide Standard -- Ch. 1: Conscience of Society
primary_topics: Chapter 1 of 'Leadership by Example: The Davide Standard' -- CJP's tribute on the retirement of Mr. Justice Antonio M. Martinez, which uses the occasion to explain what the life of a Supreme Court justice actually demands and why the Court must be, in Justice Frankfurter's phrase, 'the conscience of society.'

The argument that a magistrate's work is unteachable and solitary: no university teaches how to be a Supreme Court justice, new appointees feel at once the god-like finality of their words, and their opinions are immortalized to be perused, criticized, damned or acclaimed long after they are gone.

The contrast between the elected, for whom current popular sentiment is the catalyst and barometer of success, and magistrates, who must live in a world of reason where logic, evidence and conscience are their only yardsticks -- a difference made possible by tenure and independence.

The distinction between the shifting winds of public emotion and the long-term public trust the Court must retain, since it commands neither army nor police nor money, and its function is not to mirror popular ideas but to teach and open vistas to enlightened opinion.
sub_topics: The opening conceit borrowed from Chief Justice Andres R. Narvasa: Justice Martinez will now return to the land of the living after being judicially entombed for one year and three months in the highest court of the land.
The catalogue of liberties a retiring justice regains -- a normal life, friends, grandchildren, flowers, and freedom from the silence every member of the Court is pledged to observe.

Anthony Lewis's line from 'Gideon's Trumpet' that a justice brings to the task only his character, intellect, education, experience, human understanding and imagination, to which CJP adds creativity, innovation, reflection and prayers.
The observation that career jurists promoted through the judicial hierarchy adjust more gently than those picked straight from private practice, the academe or the nonjudicial branches of government.
The god-like finality of the Court's words: decisions right or wrong are reviewed by no other agency of government, but are immortalized in books for later judgment.
The accountability contrast: members of Congress answer to constituents and cabinet members to the President, who answers to the people, while magistrates answer to reason alone.

Tenure and independence as the constitutional guarantees that let justices withstand temporary political passions, act without fear of electoral rejection or presidential rebuff, and decide free of parochial ties and prejudices.

The essence of the craft: the search for principles and doctrines, with cases won by reasoned argument from legal principles and precedents rather than by votes, popularity, compromise, friendship, vote-trading or pecuniary considerations.
The qualification that the Court is not averse to public opinion, being effective only so long as it retains the faith and trust of the public, since it can enforce nothing by itself.
The demand made of critics: to concede the Court's good faith, wisdom, probity and diligence even when disagreeing, and to accept that its role is to teach rather than to mirror.
The test of a magistrate's mettle -- the capacity to stand by convictions when the mob rages, threatens families and chants slogans of hate -- and the definition of conscience that underlies it.

The closing farewell: Martinez's stint was all too brief, but his cadenced responses, scholarly ponencias, industry and passion for truth and fairness enriched Philippine jurisprudence and left an imprint on CJP's memory of great jurists.

stances.claim: Magistrates, unlike elected officials, must live in a world of reason where logic, evidence and conscience are their only yardsticks, and the permanency of tenure and independence granted by the Constitution is what makes such deciding possible.
stances.rhetorical_move: structural contrast between the accountability of the elected and the insulation of the appointed, with tenure cast as a functional necessity rather than a privilege

stances.claim: The search for principles and doctrines is the very essence and bedrock of the work of a jurist: cases are won by reasoned argument from legal principles and precedents, never by popular palatability, compromise, friendship or vote-trading among justices.
stances.rhetorical_move: naming and repudiating the imagined alternative -- quoting the bargain 'I vote with you in this case on condition that you vote with me in this other case' in order to disown it

stances.claim: The Court must be effective through public trust rather than public favor, distinguishing the shifting winds of public emotion from long-term institutional esteem, because its function is not to mirror popular ideas but to teach and to open vistas to enlightened opinion.
stances.rhetorical_move: concession-then-distinction: granting that the Court is powerless without popular support, then separating durable trust from momentary sentiment

stances.claim: The test of the magistrates' mettle is their capacity to stand by their convictions when the mob rages against them, threatens their families and chants slogans of hate, for that is the nature of conscience.
stances.rhetorical_move: definition-as-argument, building the standard out of Frankfurter's phrase 'the conscience of society' and then spelling out what conscience does

notable_anecdotes: CJP borrows Chief Justice Narvasa's image to open the tribute, telling Justice Martinez he will now return to the land of the living after being judicially entombed for one year and three months in the highest court of the land.

He lists what the retiring justice regains the next day -- the company of friends, his grandchildren, the freedom to smell the flowers any day, and release from the silence every member of the Court is pledged to observe.
He quotes Anthony Lewis's 'Gideon's Trumpet' on what a justice brings to the task, and adds that thereafter a justice relies on creativity, innovation, reflection and prayers.

He notes quietly that he himself belongs to the group picked straight from private practice, the academe or the nonjudicial branches, for whom the adjustment to the Court's lonely perch was sudden and unexpected.
He recalls colleagues telling him that something does happen when they don the robes of this Court -- the immediate realization of the god-like finality of their words and actions.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 1 of 'Leadership by Example: The Davide Standard' reproduces Panganiban's tribute at the retirement of Mr. Justice Antonio M. Martinez, opening with Chief Justice Andres R. Narvasa's image of a justice returning to the land of the living after being judicially entombed, and listing the ordinary liberties the retiring magistrate regains, including release from the silence every member of the Court is pledged to observe. From that occasion he turns to the nature of the office: no university on earth teaches a course on how to be a Supreme Court justice, and, quoting Anthony Lewis's 'Gideon's Trumpet,' a justice brings only his character, intellect, education, experience, human understanding and imagination, relying thereafter on creativity, innovation, reflection and prayers. He notes that career jurists adjust more easily than those picked straight from private practice, the academe or the nonjudicial branches, yet all feel at once the god-like finality of decisions no other agency may review. Where elected officials answer to current popular sentiment, magistrates must live in a world of reason where logic, evidence and conscience are their only yardsticks, a discipline made possible by the permanency of tenure and the independence the Constitution grants. The search for principles and doctrines, he argues, is the essence and bedrock of a jurist's work, and cases are won by reasoned argument rather than by popularity, compromise, friendship or vote-trading. Conceding that the Court is effective only while it keeps the public's faith, since it commands neither army, police nor money, he distinguishes the shifting winds of public emotion from long-term institutional trust and insists that the Court's function is not to mirror popular ideas but to teach and open vistas to enlightened opinion. Invoking Frankfurter's phrase that the Court is 'the conscience of society,' he defines the test of a magistrate's mettle as standing by convictions when the mob rages, and closes by mourning Martinez's too-brief stint and praising his scholarly ponencias and passion for truth and fairness.
